R^2 = \frac{SS_{\text{Model}}}{SS_{\text{Total}}}

ssb / sst

[1] 0.3730855


R^2 = 0.3731, matching the regression summary’s Multiple R-squared: 0.3731.
In empirical psychology, we rely on linear models not because reality is genuinely linear, but because linear models provide robust approximations of directional tendencies.
More generally, decomposing variation into what a model explains and what remains in its residuals is not unique to regression. It is a useful way to assess almost any model fitted to observed data, including the machine-learning models that have become so popular. Ideally, a learning algorithm explains more of the systematic variation while reducing the residual variation it cannot fit. Understanding this perspective can help when you later encounter other statistical models, statistical learning, or machine learning.
This is why psychological researchers often use linear models even when they know that relationships in the real world are more complicated. A person’s magical ability might not increase by the same amount with every additional year of age; perhaps growth accelerates until someone becomes a wizard at age 30 and then levels off. A linear model may not fit that curve exactly, but it can still support a useful approximation such as: before age 30, each additional year is associated with a modest increase in magical ability.
In much of traditional psychological statistics, linear models are therefore not used primarily to make perfectly accurate predictions. They are often used to obtain a rough, interpretable description of how variables are related.14
For precise prediction, we may be limited by sample size and by the information lost when inferring from a sample to a population. At present, psychology and related fields often focus more on describing and discovering phenomena to test theories than on predicting individual human thoughts and behavior. Moving toward reliable prediction may require further statistical advances that let researchers fit realistic models more accurately and at lower cost.


3.3.7 r, R-squared, and Eta-squared
Why is the regression determination coefficient named R^2?15
Look at our bivariate correlation from our first touch:

cor(df1.1$iden_n, df1.1$magic_score)

[1] 0.6108072



cor(df1.1$iden_n, df1.1$magic_score)^2

[1] 0.3730855



ssb / sst

[1] 0.3730855


In bivariate regression, R^2 is literally the square of Pearson’s r! Lowercase r represents the correlation between two raw variables; uppercase R represents the correlation between model predictions \hat{y} and raw outcome scores y: In our example these correlations are numerically equal, but they describe different pairs of quantities: lowercase r is the predictor–outcome correlation, while uppercase R is the correlation between the model’s predictions and the observed outcome. With multiple predictors, these are generally no longer the same.

cor(predict(lm1), df1.1$magic_score)

[1] 0.6108072


In ANOVA, the effect size \eta^2 is defined as the proportion of total variance explained by the factor:16
\eta^2 = \frac{SS_{\text{Between}}}{SS_{\text{Total}}}

rstatix::eta_squared(aov1)

     iden 
0.3730855 

ssb / sst

[1] 0.3730855


\eta^2 = r^2 = R^2 = 0.3731! They are one and the same. In this one-predictor example, the factor’s explained share of variance is numerically the same as r^2. Because it is standardized, this squared association is not expressed in the raw score units and can be used to compare effect magnitudes across measures. Correlation coefficients are accordingly a common source of effect sizes in meta-analysis.17






Note 3.2: Extension: Why Can We Code Helicopter and Bag People as 0 and 1?



In our first touch, we converted the categorical identity variable—Helicopter versus Bag—into a variable coded 0 and 1 for Pearson’s correlation. In the regression model, we used exactly the same coding. Representing a category with numeric indicator values is called dummy coding; we will study this coding method in more detail in the next chapter.
Chapter 3 has treated the two-level factor as a special kind of equally spaced numeric predictor. But if we assign different numbers, do we not change the distance between the two predictor values? Why, then, should the result remain the same?
One way to investigate is to use arbitrary codes, provided the Helicopter and Bag groups receive different values. We have already created such a variable:

## Create an arbitrarily coded variable
df1.1$iden_nn <- c(rep(233, 50), rep(7788, 50))
lm2 <- lm(magic_score ~ iden_nn, df1.1)
df1.1$magic_score_pre2 <- predict(lm2)

## Compare the predicted values and their frequencies
 table(df1.1$magic_score_pre)


81.2395315718874 95.2943932427269 
              50               50 

table(df1.1$magic_score_pre2)


81.2395315718874 95.2943932427269 
              50               50 


The two sets of predicted scores are identical: under either coding scheme, OLS predicts the sample mean of each group.18 The original 0/1 coding and the arbitrary 233/7788 coding each produce the same two predicted values, with 50 people at each value.
Why? OLS chooses the prediction that minimizes the sum of squared distances between the observed scores and the fitted value. Within a group, the constant that minimizes the sum of squared deviations is the group’s sample mean. Changing the numeric labels moves the groups horizontally on a plot, but it does not change the vertical fitted value—the group mean—assigned to either group.
The coefficient and its standard error also change together. For a simple regression slope, SE(b)=\sqrt{MSE/\sum(x-\bar{x})^2}. The denominator accounts for how far apart the predictor values are. If we increase that distance, the slope is rescaled correspondingly, and its standard error is rescaled as well. The resulting t-test of whether the slope equals zero is unchanged.








CautionCaution: Statistical Tests vs. Causal Inference



You may have noticed that I have used the terms “predictor” and “outcome,” whereas introductory t-tests and ANOVAs often use “independent variable” and “dependent variable.” In psychology courses, the latter pair is frequently introduced in the context of causal relationships.
This can lead to a dangerous misunderstanding: if a t-test or ANOVA analyzes an independent variable and a dependent variable, perhaps the statistical test can tell us how one variable causes or affects the other.19 But after this chapter, you should recognize that these tests are simply different ways of touching the same elephant. The statistical model itself cannot determine whether the elephant is wild or domesticated. Causal inference comes from the logic of the research design, not from the name of the statistical model.
Statistics tests covariation and variance partitioning; only an appropriate research design justifies causal claims. Think back to research methods or experimental psychology: what assumptions must a design satisfy before we can interpret an association causally? Longitudinal data, instrumental variables, and other methods advertised as tools for causal inference each try—under particular assumptions and to varying degrees—to address that design problem. The method name alone does not settle the causal question.








NoteExtension: Does the Dependent Variable Require a Normal Distribution?



Earlier I said that this book would not spend excessive time listing every assumption for every statistical procedure. One reason is that most of the tests in this book are different versions of the same elephant. If the models are mathematically equivalent, their statistical assumptions should be related as well.
Consider a question that I discussed with Dr. Yujun Li. Textbooks often say that, for ANOVA and the t-test, the dependent variable should be normally distributed within each group. In regression, however, the usual statement is that the residuals—the e in the equation below—should be normally distributed. How can these apparently different requirements be reconciled?
We can begin from the regression decomposition:
y = \hat{y} + e
Here, \hat{y} is the group mean. The observed outcome is therefore the group mean plus random error, and the prediction and residual are independent. Because:
\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1x
the predictor x and residual e are independent as well. When x represents our identity coding, this means that the identity code should not alter the value or distribution of the residual. Each individual’s score is a group mean plus one draw from the residual distribution. In a sufficiently large sample, those residual draws should follow the normal distribution assumed by the model.
Since the group means are constants, the within-group outcome distribution can be understood as an equivalent translation of the residual distribution. Thus, requiring normally distributed outcomes within each group is, in this simple setting, another way of expressing the regression requirement that residuals are normally distributed.20


And with that, our elephant-touching expedition is essentially complete. Writing this chapter took much longer than I expected. I wonder whether you felt any pleasure while tracing the same elephant from all these different directions. It took me five or six years to gradually understand why this elephant is an elephant.
I cannot promise that the methods described above exhaust every possible way of touching it. My hope is that readers will not merely memorize that these procedures are related, but will feel how the different hands meet and eventually converge on one animal. There is a particular beauty in this kind of statistical derivation—perhaps not unlike proving that wave mechanics and matrix mechanics are equivalent in physics.
On your future statistical travels, you may encounter unfamiliar methods and new research problems. If you can reach a point where the elephant is not in your hand but remains in your mind, learning and reasoning will become much easier. As the old phrase goes, “The greatest sound is barely audible; the greatest form is formless.” This elephant is not the t-test, not ANOVA, not correlation, and not regression. It is the statistical logic that connects your understanding of all of them. Once you see that, you can master the kung fu without resorting to self-castration.21
When we view ANOVA and regression as different ways of touching the same elephant, we call the framework the General Linear Model (GLM). It is one of the principal stepping stones from undergraduate psychological statistics to so-called advanced psychological statistics.

title: 4  Enter the Blank Person! — Coding Multi-Level Categorical Predictors
text:
4.1 One-Way ANOVA with Three Levels in Action
Back when I was in elementary school, a wildly popular game swept through my peers. Its Chinese title carried an oddly charming cadence, Children Fighting Together 2 (《小朋友齐打交2》), known internationally as Little Fighter 2 (https://www.lf2.net/). I recently searched online and was delighted to find that an official-looking website still lingers on the web. I warmly recommend curious readers try it out (though do remember to come back and finish this book).
I bring up this arcade classic for two reasons: first, it was ridiculously fun; second, among its colorful roster of martial artists, there was a peculiar character whom I always called the “Blank Person” (Template). Unlike the other warriors, the Blank Person possessed no flashy magical abilities or special combo moves—only bare-knuckle punches and kicks. Amidst the vibrant cast, this minimalist, monochrome figure felt delightfully stark and out of place.
Cruel as it sounds, in research design, such a Blank Person is the born-to-be, consummate control group. Think about it: we already have Helicopter People and Bag People, and we wish to evaluate their magical talent. What we urgently need is a cohort of people who possess zero gender self-identity, yet are functional human beings with all standard baseline capabilities. That way, we can isolate and evaluate the unique impact of each identity on magical talent.
Without further ado, let us add a cohort of Blank People into our ongoing dataset:
Let’s inspect their descriptive distributions:
Now our data is assembled, and it is time for analysis. What is our research hypothesis? Following our logic from earlier chapters, a natural hypothesis is that differences in magical talent exist among Helicopter People, Bag People, and Blank People:
\mu_{\text{Helicopter}} \ne \mu_{\text{Bag}} \ne \mu_{\text{Blank}}
The corresponding null hypothesis states that all three groups share identical magical talent:
H_0: \mu_{\text{Helicopter}} = \mu_{\text{Bag}} = \mu_{\text{Blank}}
Any seasoned student will recognize this immediately as a classic one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). While we used ANOVA in Chapter 3 to compare two groups, real-world textbooks typically showcase factors with three or more levels—precisely because ANOVA shines where the t-test cannot tread, evaluating omnibus differences across three or more groups simultaneously.
Let’s run the ANOVA:

4.2 Coding: The Magic of Transforming Categories into Continuous Predictors
To analyze differences among three groups via linear regression, our predictor is an unordered categorical variable with three levels. The primary hurdle is: how do we feed a multi-level categorical variable into a linear regression model? We touched upon this in Chapter 3 (Tip 3.1 and Tip 3.2), but back then our factor had only two levels. Now, with the intrusion of the Blank Person, our factor has three levels. What should we do?
In Chapter 2 and 3, we assigned numeric values to our two groups: Helicopter = 0, Bag = 1. A naive, instinctive impulse is simply to extend that sequence: let Blank Person = 2. Will this work? Let’s test it:

df4.1$iden_n <- c(rep(0, 50), rep(1, 50), rep(2, 50))
my.lm4.1 <- lm(magic_score ~ iden_n, df4.1)

Evidently, it does not. In Chapter 3, we proved that model fit in regression should match the ANOVA omnibus test. Yet here, the regression model reports F(1, 148) = 43.41, p = 7.296 \times 10^{-10}—completely at odds with our ANOVA result from Section 4.1 (F = 35.415). Where did things go wrong?
As emphasized earlier, a two-level categorical variable can be treated as a special “interval” variable because two points define exactly one distance. But with three groups, there are three pairwise distances: Helicopter-to-Bag, Bag-to-Blank, and Helicopter-to-Blank. Are these three distances equal? Absolutely not! Assigning \{0, 1, 2\} artificially forces the distance between Helicopter and Blank to be exactly twice the distance between Helicopter and Bag. This unwarranted geometric constraint distorts the model.
In Tip 3.2, we noted that regardless of how a binary variable is coded, OLS regression always predicts the respective group means. What about this model?

Suppose we keep D_1 (Helicopter = 0, Bag = 1, capturing the difference between Bag and Helicopter via b_1), and create a second variable D_2 (Helicopter = 0, Blank = 1, capturing the difference between Blank and Helicopter via b_2):

Note 4.1: Extension: Are Planned Comparisons Follow-Ups to One-Way ANOVA? What about Post-Hoc Comparisons?



Many statistics courses follow a familiar sequence: first teach or conduct a one-way ANOVA, then teach or conduct comparisons among its levels. As a result, I used to think—and I know other people do too—that ANOVA is the starting point of all analysis: after the omnibus test, we begin to further examine its results. For example, having found a significant difference in magical talent among Helicopter People, Bag People, and Blank People, we might then ask whether Helicopter People differ from Bag People, whether Bag People differ from Blank People, and whether Helicopter People differ from Blank People.
Are these not exactly the hypotheses we can test using dummy coding? Moreover, the set of dummy-coded predictors can jointly test whether the three groups differ at all. Does this mean these planned comparisons, taken together, are one-way ANOVA—and that after a significant ANOVA we can use them to explain its results?
A statistically savvy reader will surely say: no, that is not right. Once the ANOVA is significant, what we should conduct is a post-hoc comparison, not a planned comparison.
So, is a post-hoc test a further analysis of the one-way ANOVA result?
In terms of workflow, yes. Looking at the words planned and post-hoc,1 a post-hoc test is conducted after the ANOVA—that is what “post-hoc” means. This also meets a reasonable empirical need: after discovering a significant omnibus difference among the levels of a factor, we naturally want to know exactly which levels differ; simply knowing that some difference exists is usually not enough. That further analysis is a post-hoc test.
A statistically savvy student may object again: isn’t the defining feature of a post-hoc test that it controls the Type I error rate?
That is true of many post-hoc procedures. But logically, a post-hoc test does not have to control Type I error. Consider Fisher’s LSD (Least Significant Difference), a post-hoc test that is a variation on the t-test. What is varied? We know that the numerator of a t-statistic is a mean difference and its denominator is the standard error of the sampling distribution. The mean difference itself is straightforward—for example, the mean for Helicopter People minus the mean for Bag People. In a one-way design with several groups, however, the standard error can take the other groups (such as Blank People) into account. The LSD standard error is:
SE = \sqrt{MS_{\text{Within}}\left(\frac{1}{n_i} + \frac{1}{n_j}\right)}
The independent-samples t-test can be regarded as a special case; with three or more groups, the procedure uses them to estimate a common standard error. What does that look like in our example?

Once again, we have inadvertently touched the elephant and glimpsed the common ground among LSD, the t-test, linear regression, and ANOVA. This also answers the question we raised in this section: compared with the isolated independent-samples t-test, our planned comparison takes the standard error contributed by the other groups into account.
Wait, weren’t we discussing post-hoc comparisons? How did we end up back at planned comparisons? Congratulations—you spotted the key point. Fisher’s LSD and the set of all possible two-group planned comparisons are essentially the same tests. The difference is simply whether they are conducted after the ANOVA.
It is not entirely wrong to say that post-hoc tests are characterized by Type I error control. Fisher’s LSD is largely retained in textbooks but has been abandoned in much empirical practice precisely because it does not control Type I error. Why does that control matter?2
Suppose we have found a difference among the three groups and then conduct three separate t-tests using \alpha = 0.05. If each test is treated separately, the probability that none makes a Type I error is 0.95^3. Therefore, the probability of at least one Type I error across the study is:

1 - 0.95^3  # The probability that all three tests avoid a Type I error is 0.95^3

[1] 0.142625


Our expected level is 0.05, but this has nearly tripled it. What happens if there are more levels? The number of comparisons appears in the exponent, so the problem can become severe. Repeated hypothesis tests without Type I error control greatly increase the chance of a false positive. Thus, in the common situation where we need to perform many tests—that is, in post-hoc testing—controlling Type I error is both necessary and important.3
The many different post-hoc procedures exist because we need to balance Type I error inflation against the loss of statistical power caused by stricter control. I do not want to spend too much time on post-hoc methods: there is no universally correct answer, and this is not the main purpose of the book. Let us look at one of the strictest and most intuitive methods: Bonferroni. Its logic is straightforward. If conducting c tests inflates the family-wise Type I error rate, limit the per-test alpha by dividing 0.05 equally among them: \alpha_{\text{per test}} = 0.05/c.
We can calculate the family-wise rate in the same way. It stays around 0.05—quite strict, indeed. But who would run 999 tests? Bonferroni is often the post-hoc procedure that most effectively heads off objections.

Now, back to planned comparisons. Does a planned test mean a comparison conducted before ANOVA?
No. We need to ask a different question: is a difference between Helicopter People and Bag People part of the broader question of whether the three groups differ? Are these questions necessarily sequential? Must we first know whether all three groups differ before we can ask whether Helicopter People and Bag People differ? If the only populations in the world were Helicopter People, Bag People, and Blank People, and I had data from all three but cared only about the difference between the first two, could I ask that question?
Mathematically, differences among all three groups and a difference between two particular groups are related. But remember that research uses statistics to test hypotheses. Planned comparisons and omnibus ANOVA may be mathematically entangled; in our research, however, we should focus on the hypothesis we have and how to test it. A planned comparison is not a subordinate part of ANOVA. It can be conducted before or after ANOVA, and it is entirely legitimate to conduct a planned comparison without running ANOVA at all. The key is whether the planned test evaluates a hypothesis motivated by the theory and research question—not whether we remembered to use it only after seeing a significant ANOVA.

4.2.2 2. Effects Coding (Deviation Coding)
At the start of this chapter, we praised Blank People as an ideal control group. But in reality, control groups are rarely pristine. Suppose that one day, the Blank People achieve political consciousness and declare that their blank identity is not an “absence of identity,” but an affirmative identity in its own right. Those treacherous Blank People have sabotaged our control group!
In real-world research—especially with demographic variables like ethnicity or nationality—a pure control group rarely exists. How can we test how each group performs relative to the average across all groups?6
The Blank People may joke that their identity is “nothing,” but nothing is still a kind of something. In the language of the old Buddhist verse, “The Bodhi tree is not a tree; the bright mirror is not a stand”: absence itself can be treated as a meaningful presence rather than a void. In less mystical terms, Blank is not necessarily the absence of an identity; it can be one identity among several. Our supposedly perfect control group has therefore escaped the control group!
This is more than a joke. When the variable of interest is a real-world demographic characteristic that researchers cannot manipulate, finding a clean control group with sufficient sample size may be impossible. In that situation, comparing each group with the overall average can be more meaningful than comparing each group with one arbitrarily selected baseline.
The word average suggests a natural question: why not compare each group’s mean magical-talent score with the grand mean across all three groups? If you think about it, the between-group variation in ANOVA—the deviations of the group means from the grand mean—is already built around this idea.
With dummy coding and Helicopter People as the reference group, the regression coefficients describe the three means this way:
\begin{align}
b_0 &= \text{mean of Helicopter People} \\
b_1 &= b_0 + (\text{Bag mean} - \text{Helicopter mean}) = \text{Bag mean} \\
b_2 &= b_0 + (\text{Blank mean} - \text{Helicopter mean}) = \text{Blank mean}
\end{align}
We can change the reference point. Instead of using the Blank mean as a baseline, let the intercept be the grand mean, then express the Bag and Helicopter means as deviations from it:
\begin{align}
b_0 &= \text{grand mean} \\
b_1 &= \text{grand mean} + (\text{Bag mean} - \text{grand mean}) \\
b_2 &= \text{grand mean} + (\text{Helicopter mean} - \text{grand mean})
\end{align}
This way, testing the regression slopes tests whether each group’s mean differs from the overall mean.
In effects coding, we set the baseline to the unweighted grand mean of all groups:
\begin{align}
b_0 &= (\hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} + \hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} + \hat{y}_{\text{Blank}}) / 3 \\
b_1 &= \hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} - b_0 \\
b_2 &= \hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} - b_0
\end{align} \tag{4.4}
Solving for the group predictions in terms of coefficients:7
\begin{align}
\hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} &= b_0 + b_1 \\
\hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} &= b_0 + b_2 \\
\hat{y}_{\text{Blank}} &= b_0 - b_1 - b_2
\end{align}
The algebra is not difficult, but it is worth doing by hand. We first substitute b_1 = \hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} - b_0 and b_2 = \hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} - b_0 into the equation for b_0. Solving the resulting system gives the three group predictions above. This is exactly the kind of derivation I recommend whenever you design a custom coding scheme: do not trust the labels alone—verify what each coefficient actually tests.
For clarity, the substitution step is:
b_0 = \frac{(b_0+b_2)+(b_0+b_1)+\hat{y}_{\text{Blank}}}{3}
Solving these equations yields the predictions above. In this coding matrix, the reference group receives -1 on both coding variables. This is the key distinction from dummy coding, where the reference group receives 0 on every coding variable.
To achieve this in regression, our coding matrix must assign -1 to the reference group:

4.2.3 3. Contrast Coding
Perhaps some readers are wondering: are dummy coding and effects coding the only available options? Of course not, dear reader—there is more! We are about to introduce a wonderfully versatile, surprisingly slimming coding gadget: contrast coding.
When we introduced dummy coding, we noted that each coding variable can represent a planned comparison between two levels of a categorical factor. But readers familiar with planned comparisons may object: a planned comparison does not have to compare only two individual levels. For example, we might want to compare the combined group of Helicopter and Bag People with the Blank People. How can dummy coding represent that hypothesis? This is where contrast coding comes in.
Some readers may find the phrase “the difference between the two groups of Helicopter and Bag People and the single group of Blank People” a little confusing. To make it more concrete, imagine a parallel universe in which the identities of Helicopter and Bag People arise from a kind of animistic religion that developed into a secular culture. People form an identity by finding a concrete object in the world and developing a spiritual connection with it. Blank People, by contrast, have an identity that grew out of anime and other two-dimensional culture. They believe that the human mind originates in nothingness; they try to strip away irrelevant cultural imagery and seek the simplest possible basis for identity. For them, that basis is “blank.”8 As researchers, we might therefore want to compare whether these two different cultural origins are associated with different magical talents.
Mathematically, how do we express such a hypothesis? If we compare two groups, our hypothesis might be:
\mu_{\text{Heli}} \ne \mu_{\text{Bag}}
By analogy, to compare Helicopter and Bag People together against Blank People, we can use the average of the first two population means and compare it with the third:9
\frac{\mu_{\text{Heli}} + \mu_{\text{Bag}}}{2} - \mu_{\text{Blank}} \ne 0
Some researchers dislike having fractions in an expression, so we can multiply both sides by 2 without changing whether the contrast equals zero:
\mu_{\text{Heli}} + \mu_{\text{Bag}} - 2\mu_{\text{Blank}} \ne 0
More generally, a planned comparison among k factor levels can be written as a weighted linear combination of population means:
L = w_1\mu_1 + w_2\mu_2 + \dots + w_k\mu_k \ne 0
For our first hypothesis, the weights are w_1=1, w_2=1, and w_3=-2. This notation may look familiar. TipFood for Thought: A Half-Formed Discussion of Planned and Post-Hoc Comparisons



In Tip 4.1, we discussed how planned and post-hoc comparisons differ and when each may be appropriate. Having introduced contrast coding, we now have a much richer toolkit for planned comparisons: in principle, we can test any linear comparison of the means of a multi-level factor.
But that is not the question I want to discuss here. The question came from a post on a social-media platform.10 In broad outline, someone described a study with a five-level independent variable: one control group, which we will call A, and four treatment groups, B, C, D, and E. The researcher is interested only in whether each treatment group differs from the control group. Can they simply run four independent-samples t-tests: A-B, A-C, A-D, and A-E?
Dear thoughtful reader, pause here and decide for yourself: is that acceptable?
From the perspective of research design, my initial reaction was that it could be reasonable. But there is no denying that four unadjusted tests fail to control the family-wise Type I error rate. This is a gray area in practice: simple-effects tests are often reported without adjustment in empirical research. A more defensible—and usually more persuasive—approach is to control the error rate with a procedure such as Bonferroni, thereby treating the set of comparisons as a family of post-hoc tests. So although, in principle, a research hypothesis should be tested with a planned comparison, in practice we may need a post-hoc correction when we conduct too many tests.
But perhaps that is not the main issue here. We have described a “post-hoc” set of four comparisons, adjusted with Bonferroni: A-B, A-C, A-D, and A-E. If these were genuinely the post-hoc comparisons following some omnibus test, what would that original test be?
The usual post-hoc procedure for a one-way ANOVA examines all pairwise mean differences among the factor’s levels. For five groups, the complete set is:
A-B,\; A-C,\; A-D,\; A-E,\; B-C,\; B-D,\; B-E,\; C-D,\; C-E,\; D-E.
In other words, it enumerates every pair of levels and tests whether their means differ.
Our four comparisons—A-B, A-C, A-D, and A-E—do not enumerate every pairwise difference. Is there an omnibus hypothesis whose complete set of pairwise comparisons consists of exactly these four tests?
Look just above: we already encountered a candidate. For the five groups A through E, consider the contrast (4,-1,-1,-1,-1). Could the four differences between A and each treatment group be viewed as the complete set of pairwise comparisons associated with that planned contrast?
Here, then, is the question I genuinely want to leave open: in the study described at the beginning, may the researcher focus only on the four control-versus-treatment comparisons? Or should they first test the contrast (4,-1,-1,-1,-1) and then proceed to the pairwise comparisons? What do you think?

4.2.3.1 Orthogonality of Contrast Variables
This introduces the golden rule of contrast coding: contrast vectors must be orthogonal.
Two contrast vectors C_1 and C_2 are orthogonal if and only if: 1. The weights within each contrast sum to zero: \sum w_{1j} = 0 and \sum w_{2j} = 0. 2. The sum of their pairwise cross-products equals zero:11
\sum_{j=1}^{k} w_{1j} w_{2j} = 0
Check our first contrast coding: - Helicopter: 1 \times 1 = 1 - Bag: 1 \times (-1) = -1 - Blank: (-2) \times 0 = 0 - Sum: 1 + (-1) + 0 = 0. Orthogonal!
Now check our flawed second contrast coding: - Helicopter: 1 \times 0 = 0 - Bag: 1 \times 1 = 1 - Blank: (-2) \times (-1) = 2 - Sum: 0 + 1 + 2 = 3 \ne 0. Non-orthogonal!
When contrasts are non-orthogonal, collinearity entangles their regression slopes: the estimate for b_1 becomes contaminated by b_2. Orthogonality guarantees that each contrast partitions an independent, additive slice of sum of squares without mutual interference.12
The algebra makes this contamination visible. For the successful orthogonal coding, the group predictions satisfy:
\begin{align}
\hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} &= b_0 + b_1 + b_2 \\
\hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} &= b_0 + b_1 - b_2 \\
\hat{y}_{\text{Blank}} &= b_0 - 2b_1 + 0b_2
\end{align}
Adding the first two equations and subtracting twice the third gives:
\hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} + \hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} - 2\hat{y}_{\text{Blank}} = 6b_1
The unwanted b_2 terms cancel because the contrasts are orthogonal. Under the non-orthogonal coding, the same calculation instead produces:
\hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} + \hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} - 2\hat{y}_{\text{Blank}} = 6b_1 + 3b_2
The coefficient we intended to test is therefore contaminated by the other contrast. In more intuitive language, the two comparisons are entangled: the comparison between Bag and Blank People partly overlaps with the comparison between the two traditional groups and Blank People. To make a contrast coefficient directly test the hypothesis it was designed to represent, the other contrast variables must not share information with it.






TipFood for Thought: How Do We Find Orthogonal Codes, and How Many Are There?



I imagine that many readers’ heads are spinning at the requirement that coding variables be orthogonal. It is all very well to say that the coding variables must be orthogonal, but after constructing the coding variable for the hypothesis I care about, do I also have to find another variable orthogonal to it? How many of my remaining brain cells will that take?
I have several pieces of good news. First, although planned comparisons are flexible, I have rarely seen them in empirical research (chuckles). Researchers often use post-hoc comparisons to indirectly describe the result they had in mind. For example, they may report that Helicopter People differ significantly from Blank People, Bag People differ significantly from Blank People, but Helicopter and Bag People do not differ significantly, and then conclude that Helicopter and Bag People together differ from Blank People.
It is important to note that these three post-hoc tests do not test the same hypothesis as our planned contrast (1,1,-2). I do not recommend that workaround. Strictly speaking, if this is your hypothesis, you should conduct the planned comparison. Quite apart from the difference in the hypotheses themselves, this post-hoc approach also sacrifices statistical power.
The second piece of good news is that when the factor has only a few levels, there are not many possible orthogonal coding systems. As summarized on this webpage, a three-level factor has only one orthogonal coding system—the one introduced above. A four-level factor has three, and a five-level factor has four. I cannot recall seeing an empirical study that used planned comparisons for a categorical variable with more than five levels.
Still, you never know. Suppose you had magical-talent data for every country in the world and wanted to compare average magical talent across continents.13 Even then, there are strategies for constructing orthogonal codes. Recall that orthogonality means independence, without overlap or entanglement. A convenient strategy is to avoid making a new contrast overlap with an earlier one. For example, after comparing Helicopter and Bag People together against Blank People, do not then compare Blank People separately with Helicopter or Bag People. Instead, construct the next coding variable to compare groups within the Helicopter-and-Bag subset.

The estimated group means remain perfectly unbiased because OLS minimization operates on each group independently.
This does not mean that imbalance is irrelevant. The regression model can still estimate each group’s mean correctly, but the meaning of the grand mean—and therefore the meaning of an effects-coded intercept or contrast—requires care.
However, a fundamental distinction emerges regarding the grand mean:

Unweighted Grand Mean: treating each group as an equal conceptual unit:

\bar{Y}_{\text{Unweighted}} = \frac{\bar{Y}_{\text{Bag}} + \bar{Y}_{\text{Heli}} + \bar{Y}_{\text{Blank}}}{3} \tag{4.5}

Weighted Grand Mean: weighting each group mean by its sample size:

\bar{Y}_{\text{Weighted}} = \frac{n_1 \bar{Y}_1 + n_2 \bar{Y}_2 + n_3 \bar{Y}_3}{n_1 + n_2 + n_3} \tag{4.6}

In standard contrast and effects coding, regression intercepts estimate the unweighted grand mean. In most psychological research, unweighted means are preferred because sample size discrepancies are typically sampling artifacts rather than meaningful population proportions.21

4.2.4.1 Unweighted: The Most Common Case
If we collected 40 Helicopter People, 50 Bag People, and 30 Blank People and someone asked for the average magical talent of the people we actually observed, we would naturally compute the ordinary mean of all 120 observations. That is a weighted mean. Yet effects coding does not automatically use that quantity: its intercept is the unweighted average of the three group means. Which one is appropriate depends on the population question we are asking.
Using the weighted mean says that the unequal sample sizes themselves carry substantive information. If Bag People genuinely make up a larger share of the population, their group mean should receive greater weight when estimating the population mean. But if the unequal sample sizes merely reflect unequal sampling effort—and we believe the three underlying populations are equally large, or do not know their relative sizes—then the unweighted mean is the appropriate target. This is why unweighted comparisons are often the natural choice in psychological research.
Let’s verify what the two quantities look like in our unbalanced sample:

  group_means2[group_means2$iden == "Blank Person", 2][, 1] * 30

When the sample is balanced, the two expressions collapse to the same number. When it is unbalanced, they answer different questions. The first asks for the average of the three group means; the second asks for the average score of all observed individuals.


4.2.4.2 Weighted: One Attempt
When should we use a weighted mean? A classic example is stratified sampling. Suppose the sizes of age groups in our magical society differ, and we sample 1% of the population from each age group. The resulting sample sizes will differ, reflecting the groups’ population proportions. In estimating the population mean, we should therefore weight each group according to its share of the population.
If that is our situation, how can we construct coding variables to test a weighted comparison? We will use the planned contrast introduced above as our starting point and derive the coding weights from the desired coefficients.
The procedure is the same logic we used throughout this chapter: decide what each coefficient should mean, write the desired group predictions in terms of those coefficients, solve the resulting linear equations, and read the coefficients back as a coding matrix. The apparently unusual fractions in the table below are not arbitrary—they are the algebraic solution to the weighted hypotheses we chose.

b_2 &= \hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} - \hat{y}_{\text{Bag}}
\end{align}

In this construction, b_1 is exactly the weighted contrast between the combined Helicopter-and-Bag mean and the Blank mean, and b_2 is exactly the Helicopter-minus-Bag difference. There is no additional scale factor in these two coefficient interpretations. The chosen coding columns are also orthogonal with respect to the observed group counts:
40(1/4)+50(1/4)+30(-3/4)=0
40(5/9)+50(-4/9)+30(0)=0
40(1/4)(5/9)+50(1/4)(-4/9)+30(-3/4)(0)=0
Thus, each column’s count-weighted sum is zero, and their count-weighted cross-product is zero. The two slope tests therefore correspond directly to the two specified comparisons.
This is the practical recipe for designing weighted coding schemes: use weights that represent the target population proportions, write down what each regression coefficient should mean, solve the resulting system of equations, and then construct the coding columns. Do not use sample counts as population weights unless the sampling design justifies that interpretation.
By mastering dummy coding, effects coding, orthogonal contrast coding, and weighted systems, you can translate any substantive theoretical hypothesis directly into the General Linear Model.

A reader might ask why we use two coding variables for a three-level factor rather than three. The three group means are represented by the regression coefficients, including the intercept: \hat y_{\text{Heli}}=b_0, \hat y_{\text{Bag}}=b_0+b_1, and \hat y_{\text{Blank}}=b_0+b_2. These are three equations for three unknown coefficients. Adding another coding variable would create four unknown coefficients for only three group means. The intercept already uses one piece of information, leaving k-1 coding variables for a k-level factor—a point closely related to degrees of freedom.↩︎
